=====sandbagging.md=====
# Sandbagging clauses — pro- and anti-sandbagging

*Citation:* Delaware/Texas practice; *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta); ABA Private Target Deal Points Study  
*Status in this library:* in force

**Pro-sandbagging** clause: buyer may recover for breach of a representation even if it knew of the inaccuracy before signing/closing. **Anti-sandbagging**: buyer may not recover for breaches it knew of. Sellers who disclose a known issue (e.g., contractor classification) in diligence and then give a clean representation subject to a pro-sandbagging clause have effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue. The seller's protection is either (i) an anti-sandbagging clause, (ii) a disclosure schedule exception to the representation, or (iii) a special indemnity with a negotiated cap — not a clean rep.
=====worker_classification_tx_irs.md=====
# Worker classification — IRS common-law test; Texas Workforce Commission; successor exposure

*Citation:* IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41 (20 factors); Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1; IRC §3509; Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134  
*Status in this library:* in force

Individuals who work exclusively for one business, on its schedule, with its tools and vehicles, paid hourly, for years, are employees under the common-law control test regardless of the label. Exposure: employer FICA/FUTA (§3509 reduced rates if non-willful), state unemployment tax, overtime under the FLSA (hourly, >40 hrs), benefits eligibility, workers' comp. In an **asset sale**, the buyer generally does not inherit the seller's pre-closing payroll-tax liabilities, but may inherit **FLSA liability as a successor** where there is substantial continuity, and will have to reclassify going forward — which is why buyers price it and demand indemnity.
=====baskets_caps.md=====
# Indemnity baskets and caps — deductible vs tipping; survival

*Citation:* ABA Deal Points Study (private targets); market summary  
*Status in this library:* in force

A **deductible** basket: seller pays only losses above the threshold. A **tipping** basket: once the threshold is crossed, seller pays from the first dollar. Market: cap ~10% of price for general reps; fundamental reps and taxes to purchase price; **a specific operational rep (like worker classification) carved out to a full-price cap is off-market and should be resisted or replaced with a sized special indemnity**. Survival 12–24 months general.

=====warn_act.md=====
# WARN Act thresholds

*Citation:* 29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1); 20 C.F.R. §639.3  
*Status in this library:* in force

WARN applies to employers with **100 or more employees** (excluding part-time) and to plant closings or mass layoffs affecting 50+ employees at a single site. A 14-employee business is **not** a covered employer; no WARN notice is required even if the buyer does not hire everyone. (Texas has no mini-WARN statute.)
=====anti_assignment_change_of_control.md=====
# Anti-assignment clauses; change of control; asset sales

*Citation:* *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §317, §322; Texas cases on 'operation of law'  
*Status in this library:* in force

A clause barring assignment 'by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise' is enforced according to its terms; an asset sale transferring the contract without consent is a breach and the transfer is void where the clause so provides. Absent such language, assignment of contract rights is generally permitted; obligations require consent only if performance is personal. A consent requirement that may be withheld 'in sole discretion' gives the counterparty leverage to renegotiate price.
=====earnout_definitions.md=====
# Earn-out drafting — EBITDA definitions and buyer control

*Citation:* Practice note; *Lazard Technology Partners v. Qinetiq*, 114 A.3d 193 (Del. 2015)  
*Status in this library:* in force

An earn-out measured by 'EBITDA as determined by Buyer under Buyer's policies' lets the buyer allocate overhead, management fees, integration costs and purchase-accounting adjustments against the target, zeroing the earn-out. Seller protections: defined accounting principles (seller's historical practices or GAAP consistently applied), exclusion of buyer overhead allocations and transaction/integration costs, covenant to operate the business in the ordinary course and not take actions with the purpose of avoiding the earn-out, information and audit rights, dispute resolution by an independent accountant, acceleration on sale of the business.
=====tx_noncompete_sale_of_business.md=====
# Texas — non-competes ancillary to the sale of a business

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50; *Marsh USA v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011); sale-of-business cases  
*Status in this library:* in force

Covenants ancillary to the sale of a business are reviewed more leniently than employment covenants but must still be reasonable in time, area and scope; courts reform unreasonable covenants (§15.51(c)). Seven years / 500 miles for a local custom-cabinetry shop is likely overbroad as to both; 3–5 years within the trade area is typical. Reformation risk means the buyer, not the seller, should care — but an overbroad covenant allocated $400k of price (see tax engagement) invites IRS scrutiny of the allocation as well.

77: ## §3.3 Required Consents — **CHANGE (schedule it; add a condition and a fallback)**
78: 
79: **As drafted:** "Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the consents listed on
80: Schedule 3.3 prior to Closing. (Schedule 3.3, as drafted by Buyer: 'None.')"
81: 
82: **"None." is false on the face of the data room.** Schedule 3.3 as we require it:
83: 
84: | # | Contract | Data room | Issue | Treatment |
85: |---|---|---|---|---|
86: | 1 | Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement, 2024–2028, 38% of revenue | §1.1 | §18: assignment barred "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" without prior written consent, "withheld in its sole discretion"; purported assignment "void" | **Consent required — closing condition** (see (d)/(e) below) |
87: | 2 | Cascade Builders framework agreement, 11% of revenue | §1.2 | Assignment permitted to a successor to substantially all assets **upon notice** | Notice item, not consent; pre-closing notice obligation |
88: | 3 | 22 residential contracts, each under $40,000 | §1.3 | Silent on assignment | Assignable per the library default; list on Schedule 3.1(c); Q8 asks whether any is personal-services |
89: | 4 | Shop lease, 7700 Burleson Rd, through 2029 | §3.1 | §22: landlord consent required, "not unreasonably withheld" | Consent item; reasonableness standard; start now |
90: 
91: The library enforces the Hensley clause as written: a clause barring assignment "by operation of law,
92: merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" is enforced according to its terms; the asset sale
93: transfer without consent is a breach and the transfer is **void** where the clause so provides; "sole
94: discretion" gives the counterparty leverage to renegotiate price
95: (`library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`: *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.);
96: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §317, §322).
97: 
98: **Value at stake (arithmetic shown):** 0.38 × $4,600,000 = $1,748,000 of revenue. Margin-consistent value:
99: $1,748,000 × 16.09% (adjusted margin) = $281,200 EBITDA × 4.19× (3,100,000 ÷ 740,000) = **$1,178,000**.
100: Cross-check on the unadjusted basis: $1,748,000 × 11.26% = $196,840 × 5.98× (3,100,000 ÷ 518,000) =
101: **$1,178,000**. Both bases converge — use ~$1.18M as the anchor for any carve-out repricing.
102: 
103: **Client status (answered 2026-10-25), and how it shapes the redline:** the consent has **not** been sought;
104: Hensley has not been told about the sale; the client and Hensley's owner have a long personal relationship
105: and the client expects a poor reaction to a corporate buyer. Sequencing consequence: the first approach must
106: be client-to-owner, before any formal letter or buyer contact. The redline therefore (i) keeps the consent
107: obligation on a seller-led, jointly-agreed script, and (ii) hard-codes a fallback so a hostile answer
108: cannot blow up the closing. Do **not** volunteer the client's expectation about Hensley's receptivity to
109: buyer's counsel (see `reply_to_buyer_counsel.md` — status only, no psychology).
110: 
111: **Replacement language:**
112: 
113: > 3.3 Required Consents. (a) Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the consents, and
114: > give the notices, listed on Schedule 3.3 prior to Closing. (b) The following are Required Consents and
115: > their receipt (or the fallback under clause (e)) is a condition to Closing: the written consent of
116: > Hensley Homes to assignment of the Master Supply Agreement (the "Hensley Consent"); and landlord consent
117: > under Section 22 of the lease of 7700 Burleson Rd (which may not be unreasonably withheld). (c) Seller
118: > shall give written notice of the Cascade Builders framework agreement assignment not later than the date
119: > required by that agreement. (d) Buyer shall reasonably cooperate with Seller in the consent process,
120: > including making Buyer's senior management available to the counterparty; neither party shall contact
121: > Hensley Homes regarding the transaction except as mutually agreed in writing. (e) If the Hensley Consent
122: > has not been obtained by the Outside Date, then, at Buyer's election: (i) Closing shall proceed, the
123: > Master Supply Agreement shall not be an Assigned Contract and shall not be a Purchased Asset, and the
124: > Purchase Price shall be reduced by the Carve-Out Adjustment of $[______] (the parties acknowledge the
125: > contract carries approximately $1,178,000 of value on the margin and multiple arithmetic set out in the
126: > disclosure memorandum, and the Carve-Out Adjustment is negotiated within $[500,000]–$[1,178,000]), with
127: > the §2.4 baseline reduced accordingly; or (ii) either party may terminate this Agreement if Buyer
128: > declines clause (e)(i). "Outside Date" means [______].
129: 
130: Drafting notes:
131: 
132: - The extract has **no closing-conditions article**, so the condition in (b) must be cross-referenced into
133:   whatever conditions article the full APA contains — flagged, not assumed.
134: - A holdback alternative was considered and is **disfavored**: it delays cash without resolving whether the
135:   buyer keeps the 38% customer; a price reduction is cleaner for the seller because it fixes the exposure at
136:   signing. If buyer insists on a holdback instead, cap it at the Carve-Out Adjustment and release on consent.
137: - For the 22 residential contracts the library default helps: absent anti-assignment language, assignment of
138:   rights is generally permitted; obligations need consent only if performance is personal
139:   (`anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`). Ceiling: 22 × $40,000 = $880,000 gross.
140: 
141: ---
142: 
143: ## §4.12 Employees and Contractors — **CHANGE (schedule the exception; do not sign a clean rep)**
144: 
145: **As drafted:** "Seller represents that all individuals providing services to the Business have been
146: properly classified as employees or independent contractors under applicable law and that Seller has
147: withheld and paid all required taxes."
148: 
149: **Why it is untrue on the seller's own file.** Data room §2.2: 9 installers on 1099, exclusive to
150: Brightline, Brightline trucks and tools, scheduled daily by the shop foreman, hourly $34–41, average 3.4
151: years, **no written contractor agreements**, $612,000 paid in 2025 (612,000 ÷ 9 = $68,000 per person). The
152: library: individuals who work exclusively for one business, on its schedule, with its tools and vehicles,
153: paid hourly, for years, are employees under the common-law control test regardless of the label
154: (`library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md`: IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41 (20 factors); Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1).
155: The client's own email says "The installers have been 1099 forever, everyone in the industry does it" —
156: industry practice is not a defense under that test.
157: 
158: **The overtime layer is no longer hypothetical — the client confirmed the hours (2026-10-25): 45–50
159: hours/week in busy season, paid straight hourly.** The library lists exposure including "overtime under the
160: FLSA (hourly, >40 hrs)". The half-time premium computation (0.5 × rate × OT hours) is the standard
161: formulation but is **not spelled out in the library — [unverified; CPA must confirm]**.
162: 
163: Illustrative exposure — planning numbers, not advice. Assumptions, stated: 3-year lookback (the limitations
164: period is not in the library — Q10); FICA 7.65%; FUTA 0.6% on first $7,000/head after credit; the number of
165: busy-season **weeks** per year is unknown (client gave hours-per-busy-week) so three scenarios are run and
166: the 20-week case is the planning figure — **the week count is an assumption, not a found fact**.
167: 
168: | Component | Arithmetic | Per year | 3-year total |
169: |---|---|---|---|
170: | Employer FICA | 7.65% × $612,000 | $46,818 | $140,454 |
171: | FUTA | 9 × $7,000 × 0.6% | $378 | $1,134 |
172: | FLSA OT premium — 12 busy wks | (5–10 hrs/wk) × ($34–41) × 0.5 × 12 | $1,020–$2,460 | $3,060–$7,380 |
173: | FLSA OT premium — 20 busy wks | same, × 20 | $1,700–$4,100 | $5,100–$12,300 |
174: | FLSA OT premium — 26 busy wks | same, × 26 | $2,210–$5,330 | $6,630–$15,990 |
175: | **3-yr totals: 12 / 20 / 26 busy weeks** | FICA + FUTA + OT layer | — | **$144,648–$148,968 / $146,688–$153,888 / $148,218–$157,578** |
176: 
177: **Not included, and all additive:** TWC/state unemployment (cited in the library, rate not in it), §3509
178: income-tax gross-up (cited, rates not in it), penalties and interest, benefits eligibility and workers'
179: comp exposure (listed in the library, unquantified). A conservative gross-up — roughly doubling the tax
180: lines — still lands under ~$243,000 for the 26-week scenario. Even so, every scenario sits **inside the
181: $310,000 escrow**; the fight is not the size of the bill, it is the carve-out (see §7.4(b)) that converts a
182: ~$145,000–$158,000 problem into a $3,100,000 one.
183: 
184: **Reconciliation — now closed.** The $68,000 average annual pay vs the confirmed 45–50 busy-week hours:
185: implied annual hours are 68,000 ÷ 41 = 1,659; ÷ 37.50 = 1,813; ÷ 34 = 2,000 → 33.2–50.0 hrs/wk over a
186: 40–50-week working year. Consistent with strong seasonality: 45–50 in busy season, less the rest of the
187: year. The client's answer explains the data; nothing was forced.
188: 
189: **Client's "they like it" point:** worker satisfaction or consent is not in the library as a defense —
190: **[unverified — not in library]** — and this memo does not rely on it. Do not brief it to the buyer as a
191: defense.
192: 
193: **Replacement language:**
194: 
195: > 4.12 Employees and Contractors. Except as set forth on Schedule 4.12, Seller represents that all
196: > individuals providing services to the Business have been properly classified as employees or independent
197: > contractors under applicable law and that Seller has withheld and paid all required taxes. Schedule 4.12
198: > discloses: nine individuals engaged as independent contractors performing installation services (data
199: > room §2.2 facts: exclusive service, Company vehicles and tools, daily scheduling by Seller's foreman,
200: > hourly compensation of $34–$41 per hour, average engagement 3.4 years, no written contractor agreements,
201: > aggregate 2025 payments of $612,000); Seller does not represent that these individuals are properly
202: > classified.
203: 
204: That disclosure kills the rep's value to the buyer for this issue — which is why buyer will push back, and
205: why the paired fallback is:
206: 
207: **Fallback (if buyer refuses the exception):** keep the clean rep but (i) flip §7.4(c) to anti-sandbagging
208: and (ii) move §4.12 back inside the §7.4(b) cap, plus (iii) a single special indemnity:
209: 
210: > 7.5 Special Indemnity — Worker Classification. Notwithstanding §7.4, Seller shall indemnify Buyer for
211: > Losses arising from the classification of the individuals disclosed on Schedule 4.12 up to a maximum of
212: > $[250,000], and Buyer's sole recourse for such Losses shall be the Escrow.
213: 
214: Sizing, shown: 26-week scenario top $157,578; a ~50% gross-up for SUTA/§3509/penalties ≈ $236,000;
215: $[250,000] covers that with headroom; escrow-only recourse eliminates the tail. The $[250,000] is a
216: bracketed proposal, not a found fact. The library blesses exactly this trade: a specific operational rep
217: "carved out to a full-price cap is off-market and should be resisted or replaced with a sized special
218: indemnity" (`library/baskets_caps.md`); and the seller's protection against sandbagging is "an
219: anti-sandbagging clause, a disclosure schedule exception to the representation, or a special indemnity with
220: a negotiated cap — not a clean rep" (`library/sandbagging.md`).
221: 
222: **Buyer-side consequence to expect (and price):** the same library notes the buyer may inherit **FLSA
223: liability as a successor** where there is substantial continuity, and must reclassify going forward — the
224: buyer will argue this to keep the carve-out. It is a reason for the sized special indemnity, not for a
225: full-price cap.
226: 
227: ---
228: 
229: ## §7.4(a) Basket — **KEEP**
230: 
231: **As drafted:** "Seller shall have no liability under 7.1 until aggregate Losses exceed $75,000 (the
232: 'Basket'), and then only for Losses in excess of the Basket [deductible]."
233: 
234: A **deductible**, not a tipping basket — the seller-favorable structure; the library draws the distinction
235: and this is the good side of it (`library/baskets_caps.md`). $75,000 ≈ 2.4% of the derived price
236: (75,000 ÷ 3,100,000), unremarkable. **Keep — and guard:** the real risk is buyer re-opening the basket by
237: carving claim types out of it ("no Basket for fraud, Fundamental Reps, §4.12 …"). Resist any Basket
238: carve-outs; a basket that exempted §4.12 would let the first dollar of a classification claim start the
239: clock against the escrow.
240: 
241: ---
242: 
243: ## §7.4(b) Cap — **CHANGE (the §4.12 carve-out is the whole fight)**
244: 
245: **As drafted:** "Seller's aggregate liability under 7.1 shall not exceed 10% of the Purchase Price (the
246: 'Cap'), except for Fundamental Representations and Section 4.12, which shall be subject to a cap equal to
247: the Purchase Price."
248: 
249: **Arithmetic:** general Cap = 10% × $3,100,000 = **$310,000** = 1.0× escrow. §4.12 cap = **$3,100,000** →
250: money exposed **beyond** the escrow = 3,100,000 − 310,000 = **$2,790,000**. Illustrative §4.12 exposure on
251: the client-confirmed hours runs **$144,648–$157,578** (3-year scenarios, §4.12 note above; up to ~$243,000
252: grossed up) — the carve-out multiplies the realistic number by roughly **13×–21×**
253: (3,100,000 ÷ 157,578 ≈ 19.7; ÷ 144,648 ≈ 21.4; against the ~$243,000 grossed-up bound ≈ 12.8).
254: 
255: The library: cap ~10% for general reps is market; fundamental reps and taxes to purchase price is market;
256: **"a specific operational rep (like worker classification) carved out to a full-price cap is off-market and
257: should be resisted or replaced with a sized special indemnity"** (`library/baskets_caps.md`). "Fundamental
258: Representations" is **not defined in the extract** (Q3) — an undefined exception to the Cap is worse than a
259: defined one.
260: 
261: **Replacement language:**
262: 
263: > 7.4(b) Seller's aggregate liability under 7.1 shall not exceed 10% of the Purchase Price (the "Cap"),
264: > except that liability for breaches of Fundamental Representations (as defined in Section 1.x — definition
265: > to be provided and narrowed, see note) shall be subject to a cap equal to the Purchase Price. Section
266: > 4.12 is subject to the Cap. [Alternative, paired with §7.5 Special Indemnity: Section 4.12 is subject to
267: > the separate cap in Section 7.5 of $[250,000], recourse limited to the Escrow.]
268: 
269: Note: "Purchase Price" in the caps should be the **Closing Payment only** — if the full APA's definition
270: sweeps in the earn-out (up to $400,000 nominal, realistically $0–$16,000) it inflates every cap for paper
271: value (Q1).
272: 
273: ---
274: 
275: ## §7.4(c) Sandbagging — **CHANGE (flip or delete)**
276: 
277: **As drafted:** "Buyer's right to indemnification shall not be affected by any knowledge acquired (or
278: capable of being acquired) by Buyer at any time, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement,
279: with respect to the accuracy or inaccuracy of any representation."
280: 
281: This is a **pro-sandbagging** clause. The library's warning is this exact fact pattern: "Sellers who
282: disclose a known issue (e.g., contractor classification) in diligence and then give a clean representation
283: subject to a pro-sandbagging clause have effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue"
284: (`library/sandbagging.md`: Delaware/Texas practice; *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta); ABA
285: Private Target Deal Points Study). So our diligence disclosure of the installers does **not** protect us
286: under this clause — only the schedule exception, the anti-sandbagging flip, or the sized special indemnity
287: does.
288: 
289: **Replacement language:**
290: 
291: > 7.4(c) Buyer shall have no right to indemnification under Section 7.1 for any Losses arising from a
292: > breach of a representation (i) disclosed on the Disclosure Schedules, or (ii) actually known to Buyer as
293: > of Closing from the data room delivered before signing.
294: 
295: (Pro-sandbagging is a market position buyer's counsel may defend; the library supports the seller's three
296: protections, and the schedule exception in §4.12 works even if this clause survives.)
297: 
298: ---
299: 
300: ## §7.4(d) Survival — **TUNE (the tail is a collection risk, not a rep problem)**
301: 
302: **As drafted:** "Survival: 18 months; §4.12 and taxes: statute of limitations plus 60 days."
303: 
304: 18 months general is within the library's market band (12–24 months, `library/baskets_caps.md`). The
305: §4.12/tax tail to SOL+60 days is longer than the 18-month escrow, and the extract does **not** say the
306: escrow is the buyer's sole recourse. So a year-3 IRS assessment is collectible outside the escrow — up to
307: the applicable Cap. Two conforming fixes (paired with whichever §4.12 structure is agreed):
308: 
309: - Sole-recourse language: for claims within the Cap/Escrow, the Escrow is Buyer's sole recourse until
310:   release.
311: - If §7.5 special indemnity is agreed: two escrow tranches — $60,000 releasing at 18 months, $250,000
312:   releasing on expiry of the §4.12 survival period (sum: 60,000 + 250,000 = $310,000 = the drafted escrow).
313: 
314: The actual SOL periods (limitation periods for payroll-tax and FLSA claims) are **not in the library —
315: [unverified]**; ask the CPA (Q10).
316: 
317: ---
318: 
319: ## §8.2 Non-Competition — **CHANGE (narrow it)**
320: 
321: **As drafted:** "Seller and Ray Brightline shall not compete in the custom cabinetry business within 500
322: miles of Austin for 7 years."
323: 
324: **Replacement language:**
325: 
326: > 8.2 Non-Competition. During the Restricted Period, Seller and Ray Brightline shall not **own or operate**
327: > a custom cabinetry fabrication business within the Restricted Area. "Restricted Period" means **five (5)
328: > years** (fallback: three) from Closing. "Restricted Area" means **Travis County and the counties
329: > contiguous to it, plus any county in which the Business performed work during the 24 months preceding
330: > Closing**. Nothing in this Section prohibits Ray Brightline from providing personal services as a
331: > consultant, or from holding a passive interest of less than 5%, to any person **outside** the Restricted
332: > Area, and does not prohibit employment by a supplier of materials.
333: 
334: **Why, even though Ray says he will sign anything.** The library: covenants ancillary to the sale of a
335: business are reviewed more leniently than employment covenants but must still be reasonable in time, area
336: and scope, and courts reform unreasonable covenants — "Seven years / 500 miles for a local custom-cabinetry
337: shop is likely overbroad as to both; 3–5 years within the trade area is typical"
338: (`library/tx_noncompete_sale_of_business.md`: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50; §15.51 reformation;
339: *Marsh USA v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)). Two traps in accepting the drafted scope as-is:
340: 
341: 1. The covenant binds **Ray personally for 7 years over a 500-mile radius**. DFW, San Antonio, Houston and
342:    Waco are within 500 miles of Austin (geometric observation — not a library fact). If "retiring" later
343:    means consulting or a small shop, he signed it away; do not rely on reformation to fix it.
344: 2. **No separate payment and no allocation for §8.2 appears anywhere in the extract** — the covenant is
345:    bare. The client's answer to Q6 was that he has no additional information on allocation; the full APA
346:    must be checked. The library flags that an overbroad covenant *with* an allocation invites IRS scrutiny
347:    of the allocation; a bare covenant at full restraint is the worst combination for the seller (full
348:    restraint, zero allocated consideration). Whether §15.50's ancillarity requirement is satisfied by a
349:    bare covenant in the same agreement is not analyzed in the library — **[unverified]**; the safe fix is a
350:    narrower covenant plus an agreed allocation.
351: 
352: Client answer used (Q4): "I'll sign whatever non-compete, I'm retiring." That answers willingness, not
353: plans — the redline still narrows, and Q4 stays open on what "retiring" means (consulting? family entities
354: in the trade?).
355: 
356: ---
357: 
358: ## §9.3 Escrow — **KEEP (amount/term), CONFORM (recourse)**
359: 
360: **As drafted:** "$310,000 (10%) for 18 months."
361: 
362: Amount and term match the drafted cap (10%) and general survival (18 months) — keep them; they are the
363: library's market parameters (`baskets_caps.md`). **But:** (i) this caption is the *only* price figure in the
364: file — it is the basis of the $3,100,000 derivation used everywhere (Q1); (ii) as extracted, nothing says
365: the escrow is the buyer's **sole recourse** for capped claims — without that, post-release claims are
366: collectible directly (see §7.4(d) note); (iii) if the §7.5 special indemnity is agreed, tranche as
367: $60,000 + $250,000 with staggered releases. Full §9 text is not in the extract — conform once provided.
368: 
369: ---
370: 
371: ## Cross-cutting items (outside the six sections but load-bearing)
372: 
373: - **No closing-conditions article in the extract.** The §3.3(b) condition must be conformed into the full
374:   APA. Flagged, not assumed.
375: - **No allocation schedule anywhere in the file** (Q6 — client has no additional information). Earn-out is
376:   realistically $0–$16,000; §8.2 is bare. Get the full APA and CPA input before signature.
377: - **Schedule 3.1(c) (Assigned Contracts) is referenced but not provided.** The 22 residential contracts,
378:   Cascade and (subject to §3.3(e)) Hensley must appear consistently across Schedules 3.1(c) and 3.3.
379: - **Permit timing (data room §4.1):** the City of Austin spray-booth permit is non-transferable and must be
380:   reapplied for (30–60 days per the data room). That collides with "sign in two weeks" if closing follows
381:   signing immediately — raise in the reply and the note to Ray.

26: ## §2.4 Earn-Out — **CHANGE (heavy)**
27: 
28: **As drafted:** "In addition to the Closing Payment, Buyer shall pay Seller an amount equal to 40% of the
29: amount by which EBITDA of the Business for the twelve months following Closing exceeds $700,000, up to a
30: maximum of $400,000. 'EBITDA' shall mean earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of
31: the Business as determined by Buyer in good faith in accordance with Buyer's accounting policies,
32: consistently applied."
33: 
34: **Arithmetic first — treat this earn-out as nearly worthless:**
35: 
36: - Maximum payout requires EBITDA of $700,000 + $400,000 ÷ 0.40 = **$1,700,000** —
37:   vs 2025 seller-prepared EBITDA $740,000 → 1,700,000 ÷ 740,000 = **2.30×** the adjusted figure. Unreachable.
38: - **Assumption, flagged:** the measurement period is "the twelve months following Closing." The closing date
39:   is not in the file, so 2025 actuals are used as a proxy throughout; this is a proxy, not a fact.
40: - Proxy, flat performance (adjusted): 0.40 × (740,000 − 700,000) = **$16,000**.
41: - Proxy, flat performance (unadjusted — buyer may disallow the $180,000 owner-salary and $42,000 "one-time"
42:   legal add-backs, data room §6.1): 740,000 − 180,000 − 42,000 = $518,000, below the floor → **$0**.
43: - If Hensley is lost (see §3.3): remaining EBITDA is $740,000 − $281,200 = **$458,800** (adjusted basis) or
44:   $518,000 − $196,840 = **$321,160** (unadjusted basis). Both are under $700,000 → earn-out **$0**.
45:   (Hensley EBITDA share: 0.38 × $4,600,000 = $1,748,000 revenue; × adjusted margin 740,000/4,600,000 = 16.09%
46:   → $281,200; × unadjusted margin 518,000/4,600,000 = 11.26% → $196,840.)
47: 
48: So plan on **$0–$16,000**, not $400,000. Do not give the earn-out value in allocation (Q6) or let it inflate
49: "total consideration" when caps are negotiated (Q1: check whether the defined "Purchase Price" includes it).
50: 
51: **Why the drafting is dangerous.** The library is squarely on point: an earn-out measured by "EBITDA as
52: determined by Buyer under Buyer's policies" lets the buyer allocate overhead, management fees, integration
53: costs and purchase-accounting adjustments against the target, zeroing the earn-out
54: (`library/earnout_definitions.md`; *Lazard Technology Partners v. Qinetiq*, 114 A.3d 193 (Del. 2015)). The
55: same memo lists the standard seller protections; the draft has none of them.
56: 
57: **Replacement language (core):**
58: 
59: > 2.4 Earn-Out. In addition to the Closing Payment, Buyer shall pay Seller an amount equal to 40% of the
60: > amount by which Adjusted EBITDA of the Business for the twelve (12) months following Closing exceeds
61: > $700,000, up to a maximum of $400,000. "Adjusted EBITDA" means EBITDA of the Business determined in
62: > accordance with the accounting principles, practices and policies used by Seller in preparing the
63: > Historical Financial Statements, consistently applied, excluding: (i) allocations of Buyer overhead,
64: > management or monitoring fees; (ii) transaction, integration and restructuring costs; and
65: > (iii) purchase-accounting adjustments and non-cash charges. The parties agree the add-backs on Schedule
66: > 2.4 (owner compensation of $180,000 and non-recurring legal fees of $42,000) are included. Buyer shall
67: > operate the Business after Closing in the ordinary course and shall not take any action with the purpose
68: > of avoiding or reducing the Earn-Out. Seller shall have information and audit rights, and disputes on
69: > Adjusted EBITDA shall be resolved by an independent accounting firm acting as expert, not arbitrator.
70: > The Earn-Out accelerates on a sale of the Business.
71: 
72: Bracketed for CPA work: the agreed add-back schedule (Schedule 2.4) must survive diligence; the seller's
73: own $740,000 is "seller-prepared" (data room §6.1) and is not audit-proof.
74: 
75: ---
76: 
77: ## §3.3 Required Consents — **CHANGE (schedule it; add a condition and a fallback)**
78: 
79: **As drafted:** "Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the consents listed on
80: Schedule 3.3 prior to Closing. (Schedule 3.3, as drafted by Buyer: 'None.')"
81: 
82: **"None." is false on the face of the data room.** Schedule 3.3 as we require it:
83: 
84: | # | Contract | Data room | Issue | Treatment |
85: |---|---|---|---|---|
86: | 1 | Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement, 2024–2028, 38% of revenue | §1.1 | §18: assignment barred "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" without prior written consent, "withheld in its sole discretion"; purported assignment "void" | **Consent required — closing condition** (see (d)/(e) below) |
87: | 2 | Cascade Builders framework agreement, 11% of revenue | §1.2 | Assignment permitted to a successor to substantially all assets **upon notice** | Notice item, not consent; pre-closing notice obligation |
88: | 3 | 22 residential contracts, each under $40,000 | §1.3 | Silent on assignment | Assignable per the library default; list on Schedule 3.1(c); Q8 asks whether any is personal-services |
89: | 4 | Shop lease, 7700 Burleson Rd, through 2029 | §3.1 | §22: landlord consent required, "not unreasonably withheld" | Consent item; reasonableness standard; start now |
90: 
91: The library enforces the Hensley clause as written: a clause barring assignment "by operation of law,
92: merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" is enforced according to its terms; the asset sale
93: transfer without consent is a breach and the transfer is **void** where the clause so provides; "sole
94: discretion" gives the counterparty leverage to renegotiate price
95: (`library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`: *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.);
96: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §317, §322).
97: 
98: **Value at stake (arithmetic shown):** 0.38 × $4,600,000 = $1,748,000 of revenue. Margin-consistent value:
99: $1,748,000 × 16.09% (adjusted margin) = $281,200 EBITDA × 4.19× (3,100,000 ÷ 740,000) = **$1,178,000**.
100: Cross-check on the unadjusted basis: $1,748,000 × 11.26% = $196,840 × 5.98× (3,100,000 ÷ 518,000) =
101: **$1,178,000**. Both bases converge — use ~$1.18M as the anchor for any carve-out repricing.
102: 
103: **Client status (answered 2026-10-25), and how it shapes the redline:** the consent has **not** been sought;
104: Hensley has not been told about the sale; the client and Hensley's owner have a long personal relationship
105: and the client expects a poor reaction to a corporate buyer. Sequencing consequence: the first approach must
106: be client-to-owner, before any formal letter or buyer contact. The redline therefore (i) keeps the consent
107: obligation on a seller-led, jointly-agreed script, and (ii) hard-codes a fallback so a hostile answer
108: cannot blow up the closing. Do **not** volunteer the client's expectation about Hensley's receptivity to
109: buyer's counsel (see `reply_to_buyer_counsel.md` — status only, no psychology).
110: 
111: **Replacement language:**
112: 
113: > 3.3 Required Consents. (a) Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the consents, and
114: > give the notices, listed on Schedule 3.3 prior to Closing. (b) The following are Required Consents and
115: > their receipt (or the fallback under clause (e)) is a condition to Closing: the written consent of
116: > Hensley Homes to assignment of the Master Supply Agreement (the "Hensley Consent"); and landlord consent
117: > under Section 22 of the lease of 7700 Burleson Rd (which may not be unreasonably withheld). (c) Seller
118: > shall give written notice of the Cascade Builders framework agreement assignment not later than the date
119: > required by that agreement. (d) Buyer shall reasonably cooperate with Seller in the consent process,
120: > including making Buyer's senior management available to the counterparty; neither party shall contact
121: > Hensley Homes regarding the transaction except as mutually agreed in writing. (e) If the Hensley Consent
122: > has not been obtained by the Outside Date, then, at Buyer's election: (i) Closing shall proceed, the
123: > Master Supply Agreement shall not be an Assigned Contract and shall not be a Purchased Asset, and the
124: > Purchase Price shall be reduced by the Carve-Out Adjustment of $[______] (the parties acknowledge the
125: > contract carries approximately $1,178,000 of value on the margin and multiple arithmetic set out in the
126: > disclosure memorandum, and the Carve-Out Adjustment is negotiated within $[500,000]–$[1,178,000]), with
127: > the §2.4 baseline reduced accordingly; or (ii) either party may terminate this Agreement if Buyer
128: > declines clause (e)(i). "Outside Date" means [______].
129: 
130: Drafting notes:
131: 
132: - The extract has **no closing-conditions article**, so the condition in (b) must be cross-referenced into
133:   whatever conditions article the full APA contains — flagged, not assumed.
134: - A holdback alternative was considered and is **disfavored**: it delays cash without resolving whether the
135:   buyer keeps the 38% customer; a price reduction is cleaner for the seller because it fixes the exposure at
136:   signing. If buyer insists on a holdback instead, cap it at the Carve-Out Adjustment and release on consent.
137: - For the 22 residential contracts the library default helps: absent anti-assignment language, assignment of
138:   rights is generally permitted; obligations need consent only if performance is personal
139:   (`anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`). Ceiling: 22 × $40,000 = $880,000 gross.
140: 
141: ---

143: ## §4.12 Employees and Contractors — **CHANGE (schedule the exception; do not sign a clean rep)**
144: 
145: **As drafted:** "Seller represents that all individuals providing services to the Business have been
146: properly classified as employees or independent contractors under applicable law and that Seller has
147: withheld and paid all required taxes."
148: 
149: **Why it is untrue on the seller's own file.** Data room §2.2: 9 installers on 1099, exclusive to
150: Brightline, Brightline trucks and tools, scheduled daily by the shop foreman, hourly $34–41, average 3.4
151: years, **no written contractor agreements**, $612,000 paid in 2025 (612,000 ÷ 9 = $68,000 per person). The
152: library: individuals who work exclusively for one business, on its schedule, with its tools and vehicles,
153: paid hourly, for years, are employees under the common-law control test regardless of the label
154: (`library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md`: IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41 (20 factors); Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1).
155: The client's own email says "The installers have been 1099 forever, everyone in the industry does it" —
156: industry practice is not a defense under that test.
157: 
158: **The overtime layer is no longer hypothetical — the client confirmed the hours (2026-10-25): 45–50
159: hours/week in busy season, paid straight hourly.** The library lists exposure including "overtime under the
160: FLSA (hourly, >40 hrs)". The half-time premium computation (0.5 × rate × OT hours) is the standard
161: formulation but is **not spelled out in the library — [unverified; CPA must confirm]**.
162: 
163: Illustrative exposure — planning numbers, not advice. Assumptions, stated: 3-year lookback (the limitations
164: period is not in the library — Q10); FICA 7.65%; FUTA 0.6% on first $7,000/head after credit; the number of
165: busy-season **weeks** per year is unknown (client gave hours-per-busy-week) so three scenarios are run and
166: the 20-week case is the planning figure — **the week count is an assumption, not a found fact**.
167: 
168: | Component | Arithmetic | Per year | 3-year total |
169: |---|---|---|---|
170: | Employer FICA | 7.65% × $612,000 | $46,818 | $140,454 |
171: | FUTA | 9 × $7,000 × 0.6% | $378 | $1,134 |
172: | FLSA OT premium — 12 busy wks | (5–10 hrs/wk) × ($34–41) × 0.5 × 12 | $1,020–$2,460 | $3,060–$7,380 |
173: | FLSA OT premium — 20 busy wks | same, × 20 | $1,700–$4,100 | $5,100–$12,300 |
174: | FLSA OT premium — 26 busy wks | same, × 26 | $2,210–$5,330 | $6,630–$15,990 |
175: | **3-yr totals: 12 / 20 / 26 busy weeks** | FICA + FUTA + OT layer | — | **$144,648–$148,968 / $146,688–$153,888 / $148,218–$157,578** |
176: 
177: **Not included, and all additive:** TWC/state unemployment (cited in the library, rate not in it), §3509
178: income-tax gross-up (cited, rates not in it), penalties and interest, benefits eligibility and workers'
179: comp exposure (listed in the library, unquantified). A conservative gross-up — roughly doubling the tax
180: lines — still lands under ~$243,000 for the 26-week scenario. Even so, every scenario sits **inside the
181: $310,000 escrow**; the fight is not the size of the bill, it is the carve-out (see §7.4(b)) that converts a
182: ~$145,000–$158,000 problem into a $3,100,000 one.
183: 
184: **Reconciliation — now closed.** The $68,000 average annual pay vs the confirmed 45–50 busy-week hours:
185: implied annual hours are 68,000 ÷ 41 = 1,659; ÷ 37.50 = 1,813; ÷ 34 = 2,000 → 33.2–50.0 hrs/wk over a
186: 40–50-week working year. Consistent with strong seasonality: 45–50 in busy season, less the rest of the
187: year. The client's answer explains the data; nothing was forced.
188: 
189: **Client's "they like it" point:** worker satisfaction or consent is not in the library as a defense —
190: **[unverified — not in library]** — and this memo does not rely on it. Do not brief it to the buyer as a
191: defense.
192: 
193: **Replacement language:**
194: 
195: > 4.12 Employees and Contractors. Except as set forth on Schedule 4.12, Seller represents that all
196: > individuals providing services to the Business have been properly classified as employees or independent
197: > contractors under applicable law and that Seller has withheld and paid all required taxes. Schedule 4.12
198: > discloses: nine individuals engaged as independent contractors performing installation services (data
199: > room §2.2 facts: exclusive service, Company vehicles and tools, daily scheduling by Seller's foreman,
200: > hourly compensation of $34–$41 per hour, average engagement 3.4 years, no written contractor agreements,
201: > aggregate 2025 payments of $612,000); Seller does not represent that these individuals are properly
202: > classified.
203: 
204: That disclosure kills the rep's value to the buyer for this issue — which is why buyer will push back, and
205: why the paired fallback is:
206: 
207: **Fallback (if buyer refuses the exception):** keep the clean rep but (i) flip §7.4(c) to anti-sandbagging
208: and (ii) move §4.12 back inside the §7.4(b) cap, plus (iii) a single special indemnity:
209: 
210: > 7.5 Special Indemnity — Worker Classification. Notwithstanding §7.4, Seller shall indemnify Buyer for
211: > Losses arising from the classification of the individuals disclosed on Schedule 4.12 up to a maximum of
212: > $[250,000], and Buyer's sole recourse for such Losses shall be the Escrow.
213: 
214: Sizing, shown: 26-week scenario top $157,578; a ~50% gross-up for SUTA/§3509/penalties ≈ $236,000;
215: $[250,000] covers that with headroom; escrow-only recourse eliminates the tail. The $[250,000] is a
216: bracketed proposal, not a found fact. The library blesses exactly this trade: a specific operational rep
217: "carved out to a full-price cap is off-market and should be resisted or replaced with a sized special
218: indemnity" (`library/baskets_caps.md`); and the seller's protection against sandbagging is "an
219: anti-sandbagging clause, a disclosure schedule exception to the representation, or a special indemnity with
220: a negotiated cap — not a clean rep" (`library/sandbagging.md`).
221: 
222: **Buyer-side consequence to expect (and price):** the same library notes the buyer may inherit **FLSA
223: liability as a successor** where there is substantial continuity, and must reclassify going forward — the
224: buyer will argue this to keep the carve-out. It is a reason for the sized special indemnity, not for a
225: full-price cap.
226: 
227: ---
228: 
229: ## §7.4(a) Basket — **KEEP**
230: 
231: **As drafted:** "Seller shall have no liability under 7.1 until aggregate Losses exceed $75,000 (the
232: 'Basket'), and then only for Losses in excess of the Basket [deductible]."
233: 
234: A **deductible**, not a tipping basket — the seller-favorable structure; the library draws the distinction
235: and this is the good side of it (`library/baskets_caps.md`). $75,000 ≈ 2.4% of the derived price
236: (75,000 ÷ 3,100,000), unremarkable. **Keep — and guard:** the real risk is buyer re-opening the basket by
237: carving claim types out of it ("no Basket for fraud, Fundamental Reps, §4.12 …"). Resist any Basket
238: carve-outs; a basket that exempted §4.12 would let the first dollar of a classification claim start the
239: clock against the escrow.
240: 
241: ---
242: 
243: ## §7.4(b) Cap — **CHANGE (the §4.12 carve-out is the whole fight)**
244: 
245: **As drafted:** "Seller's aggregate liability under 7.1 shall not exceed 10% of the Purchase Price (the
246: 'Cap'), except for Fundamental Representations and Section 4.12, which shall be subject to a cap equal to
247: the Purchase Price."
248: 
249: **Arithmetic:** general Cap = 10% × $3,100,000 = **$310,000** = 1.0× escrow. §4.12 cap = **$3,100,000** →
250: money exposed **beyond** the escrow = 3,100,000 − 310,000 = **$2,790,000**. Illustrative §4.12 exposure on
251: the client-confirmed hours runs **$144,648–$157,578** (3-year scenarios, §4.12 note above; up to ~$243,000
252: grossed up) — the carve-out multiplies the realistic number by roughly **13×–21×**
253: (3,100,000 ÷ 157,578 ≈ 19.7; ÷ 144,648 ≈ 21.4; against the ~$243,000 grossed-up bound ≈ 12.8).
254: 
255: The library: cap ~10% for general reps is market; fundamental reps and taxes to purchase price is market;
256: **"a specific operational rep (like worker classification) carved out to a full-price cap is off-market and
257: should be resisted or replaced with a sized special indemnity"** (`library/baskets_caps.md`). "Fundamental
258: Representations" is **not defined in the extract** (Q3) — an undefined exception to the Cap is worse than a
259: defined one.
260: 
261: **Replacement language:**
262: 
263: > 7.4(b) Seller's aggregate liability under 7.1 shall not exceed 10% of the Purchase Price (the "Cap"),
264: > except that liability for breaches of Fundamental Representations (as defined in Section 1.x — definition
265: > to be provided and narrowed, see note) shall be subject to a cap equal to the Purchase Price. Section
266: > 4.12 is subject to the Cap. [Alternative, paired with §7.5 Special Indemnity: Section 4.12 is subject to
267: > the separate cap in Section 7.5 of $[250,000], recourse limited to the Escrow.]
268: 
269: Note: "Purchase Price" in the caps should be the **Closing Payment only** — if the full APA's definition
270: sweeps in the earn-out (up to $400,000 nominal, realistically $0–$16,000) it inflates every cap for paper
271: value (Q1).
272: 
273: ---
274: 
275: ## §7.4(c) Sandbagging — **CHANGE (flip or delete)**
276: 
277: **As drafted:** "Buyer's right to indemnification shall not be affected by any knowledge acquired (or
278: capable of being acquired) by Buyer at any time, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement,
279: with respect to the accuracy or inaccuracy of any representation."
280: 
281: This is a **pro-sandbagging** clause. The library's warning is this exact fact pattern: "Sellers who
282: disclose a known issue (e.g., contractor classification) in diligence and then give a clean representation
283: subject to a pro-sandbagging clause have effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue"
284: (`library/sandbagging.md`: Delaware/Texas practice; *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta); ABA
285: Private Target Deal Points Study). So our diligence disclosure of the installers does **not** protect us
286: under this clause — only the schedule exception, the anti-sandbagging flip, or the sized special indemnity
287: does.
288: 
289: **Replacement language:**
290: 
291: > 7.4(c) Buyer shall have no right to indemnification under Section 7.1 for any Losses arising from a
292: > breach of a representation (i) disclosed on the Disclosure Schedules, or (ii) actually known to Buyer as
293: > of Closing from the data room delivered before signing.
294: 
295: (Pro-sandbagging is a market position buyer's counsel may defend; the library supports the seller's three
296: protections, and the schedule exception in §4.12 works even if this clause survives.)
297: 
298: ---
299: 
300: ## §7.4(d) Survival — **TUNE (the tail is a collection risk, not a rep problem)**
301: 
302: **As drafted:** "Survival: 18 months; §4.12 and taxes: statute of limitations plus 60 days."
303: 
304: 18 months general is within the library's market band (12–24 months, `library/baskets_caps.md`). The
305: §4.12/tax tail to SOL+60 days is longer than the 18-month escrow, and the extract does **not** say the
306: escrow is the buyer's sole recourse. So a year-3 IRS assessment is collectible outside the escrow — up to
307: the applicable Cap. Two conforming fixes (paired with whichever §4.12 structure is agreed):
308: 
309: - Sole-recourse language: for claims within the Cap/Escrow, the Escrow is Buyer's sole recourse until
310:   release.
311: - If §7.5 special indemnity is agreed: two escrow tranches — $60,000 releasing at 18 months, $250,000
312:   releasing on expiry of the §4.12 survival period (sum: 60,000 + 250,000 = $310,000 = the drafted escrow).
313: 
314: The actual SOL periods (limitation periods for payroll-tax and FLSA claims) are **not in the library —
315: [unverified]**; ask the CPA (Q10).
316: 
317: ---
318: 
319: ## §8.2 Non-Competition — **CHANGE (narrow it)**
320: 
321: **As drafted:** "Seller and Ray Brightline shall not compete in the custom cabinetry business within 500
322: miles of Austin for 7 years."
323: 
324: **Replacement language:**
325: 
326: > 8.2 Non-Competition. During the Restricted Period, Seller and Ray Brightline shall not **own or operate**
327: > a custom cabinetry fabrication business within the Restricted Area. "Restricted Period" means **five (5)
328: > years** (fallback: three) from Closing. "Restricted Area" means **Travis County and the counties
329: > contiguous to it, plus any county in which the Business performed work during the 24 months preceding
330: > Closing**. Nothing in this Section prohibits Ray Brightline from providing personal services as a
331: > consultant, or from holding a passive interest of less than 5%, to any person **outside** the Restricted
332: > Area, and does not prohibit employment by a supplier of materials.
333: 
334: **Why, even though Ray says he will sign anything.** The library: covenants ancillary to the sale of a
335: business are reviewed more leniently than employment covenants but must still be reasonable in time, area
336: and scope, and courts reform unreasonable covenants — "Seven years / 500 miles for a local custom-cabinetry
337: shop is likely overbroad as to both; 3–5 years within the trade area is typical"
338: (`library/tx_noncompete_sale_of_business.md`: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50; §15.51 reformation;
339: *Marsh USA v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)). Two traps in accepting the drafted scope as-is:
340: 
341: 1. The covenant binds **Ray personally for 7 years over a 500-mile radius**. DFW, San Antonio, Houston and
342:    Waco are within 500 miles of Austin (geometric observation — not a library fact). If "retiring" later
343:    means consulting or a small shop, he signed it away; do not rely on reformation to fix it.
344: 2. **No separate payment and no allocation for §8.2 appears anywhere in the extract** — the covenant is
345:    bare. The client's answer to Q6 was that he has no additional information on allocation; the full APA
346:    must be checked. The library flags that an overbroad covenant *with* an allocation invites IRS scrutiny
347:    of the allocation; a bare covenant at full restraint is the worst combination for the seller (full
348:    restraint, zero allocated consideration). Whether §15.50's ancillarity requirement is satisfied by a
349:    bare covenant in the same agreement is not analyzed in the library — **[unverified]**; the safe fix is a
350:    narrower covenant plus an agreed allocation.
351: 
352: Client answer used (Q4): "I'll sign whatever non-compete, I'm retiring." That answers willingness, not
353: plans — the redline still narrows, and Q4 stays open on what "retiring" means (consulting? family entities
354: in the trade?).
355: 
356: ---
357: 
358: ## §9.3 Escrow — **KEEP (amount/term), CONFORM (recourse)**
359: 
360: **As drafted:** "$310,000 (10%) for 18 months."
361: 
362: Amount and term match the drafted cap (10%) and general survival (18 months) — keep them; they are the
363: library's market parameters (`baskets_caps.md`). **But:** (i) this caption is the *only* price figure in the
364: file — it is the basis of the $3,100,000 derivation used everywhere (Q1); (ii) as extracted, nothing says
365: the escrow is the buyer's **sole recourse** for capped claims — without that, post-release claims are
366: collectible directly (see §7.4(d) note); (iii) if the §7.5 special indemnity is agreed, tranche as
367: $60,000 + $250,000 with staggered releases. Full §9 text is not in the extract — conform once provided.
368: 
369: ---
370: 
371: ## Cross-cutting items (outside the six sections but load-bearing)
372: 
373: - **No closing-conditions article in the extract.** The §3.3(b) condition must be conformed into the full
374:   APA. Flagged, not assumed.
375: - **No allocation schedule anywhere in the file** (Q6 — client has no additional information). Earn-out is
376:   realistically $0–$16,000; §8.2 is bare. Get the full APA and CPA input before signature.
377: - **Schedule 3.1(c) (Assigned Contracts) is referenced but not provided.** The 22 residential contracts,
378:   Cascade and (subject to §3.3(e)) Hensley must appear consistently across Schedules 3.1(c) and 3.3.
379: - **Permit timing (data room §4.1):** the City of Austin spray-booth permit is non-transferable and must be
380:   reapplied for (30–60 days per the data room). That collides with "sign in two weeks" if closing follows
381:   signing immediately — raise in the reply and the note to Ray.

Header: Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product. To: Ray Brightline (Brightline Cabinetry LLC). From: deal counsel. Date: 2026-10-25.

# Note for Ray — the three things that can cost you money after closing

**Privileged & confidential — attorney work product**
From: deal counsel · To: Ray Brightline, Brightline Cabinetry LLC
Re: buyer's draft APA (Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC) — plain-English read before you sign
Client answers of 2026-10-25 are reflected below; where we still lack a fact, it says so.

Ray,

You asked us to "just tell me if there's anything in here that bites me later." Here are the three
things that can cost you money **after** closing, in order of size. All dollar figures assume a
**Purchase Price of $3,100,000**, which we derived from the buyer's own §9.3 — "$310,000 (10%)"
escrow → $310,000 ÷ 0.10 = $3,100,000. The file never states the price; if $3.1M is wrong
(Q1 in `QUESTIONS.md`), every number below moves, but the problems are the same.

Key deal numbers used throughout (all derived from the draft):

| Item | Where | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Purchase Price (derived) | §9.3 | **$3,100,000** |
| Escrow, 18 months | §9.3 | $310,000 |
| General indemnity cap (10%) | §7.4(b) | $310,000 |
| Cap for §4.12 + "Fundamental Representations" | §7.4(b) | **$3,100,000** (full price) |
| Basket (deductible) | §7.4(a) | first $75,000 not payable (~2.4% of price) |

---

## 1. The 1099 installers — the biggest number with your name on it

You told us: "The installers have been 1099 forever, everyone in the industry does it," and "they
like it." We hear you. But two things are separate:

- **The legal question.** Your own data room (§2.2) describes the nine installers as "working
  exclusively for Brightline, using Brightline trucks and tools, scheduled daily by the shop
  foreman, paid hourly ($34–41/hr), for an average of 3.4 years." The reference library says that
  exact fact pattern makes people **employees under the common-law control test regardless of the
  label** (`library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md`: IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41 20 factors; Treas. Reg.
  §31.3121(d)-1; IRC §3509; Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134). "Everyone in the industry
  does it" and "the workers like it" do **not** appear in the library as defenses —
  **[unverified — not in library]** — so do not offer either to the buyer as a defense.
- **The drafting question.** As drafted, the APA routes that problem to you personally after
  closing:
  - **§4.12** makes you *represent* that everyone is properly classified and all taxes were paid.
    On your own data room's facts, that rep is not true as written.
  - **§7.4(b)** caps §4.12 breaches at the **full purchase price — $3,100,000**, not the $310,000
    general cap. Money beyond the $310,000 escrow (3,100,000 − 310,000 = **$2,790,000**) would
    come from you directly, not just out of escrow.
  - **§7.4(c)** says the buyer's **knowledge changes nothing** — even though we will have told
    them about this in diligence, they can still claim against you. The library is blunt: a seller
    who discloses the classification issue and then gives a clean rep under this kind of clause
    "has effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue" (`library/sandbagging.md`).
  - **§7.4(d)** keeps §4.12 alive to the **statute of limitations plus 60 days** — likely years —
    while the escrow releases at **18 months** (§9.3). The claim outlives the escrow; it comes
    after you personally. (The limitations period is not in the library — **[unverified — not in
    library]** — Q10 asks your CPA to confirm it.)

**What the problem probably actually costs (arithmetic shown, all flagged):** employer FICA
7.65% × $612,000 of 1099 pay = $46,818/yr × 3 = $140,454; FUTA 9 × $7,000 × 0.6% = $378/yr × 3 =
$1,134; overtime premium for 5–10 OT hrs/wk at $34–41/hr over 12/20/26 busy-season weeks =
$3,060–$15,990. Three-year scenarios: **$144,648–$157,578**; adding a 50% allowance for the items
the library lists but doesn't quantify (SUTA, §3509 gross-up, penalties) gives ≈ **$236,400**.
The 7.65%/0.6% rates, the 3-year window, and the busy-week count are assumptions your CPA must
confirm (Q10). Your confirmed 45–50 busy-season hours fit the pay data: $68,000 average annual
pay ÷ $37.50/hr midpoint = 1,813 hrs/yr = 33–50 hrs/wk over a 40–50-week year — busy-season-heavy,
consistent with what you told us. Nothing here was forced.

**The point:** the real bill is roughly $150,000–$240,000. The draft lets the buyer claim up to
$3,100,000 for it — about **13×–21×** the realistic number (3,100,000 ÷ 236,367 ≈ 13.1; ÷ 144,648
≈ 21.4). The library calls a full-price cap on a worker-classification rep **"off-market"** and
says to replace it with a **sized special indemnity** (`library/baskets_caps.md`). That is exactly
our ask: an exception on Schedule 4.12, or a special indemnity capped at **$[250,000], escrow-only**
(the bracket is our proposed number, not the buyer's).

## 2. Hensley Homes — 38% of your revenue, and the buyer wrote "consents: None."

The Hensley MSA (§18) says neither side may assign it "whether by operation of law, merger, sale
of assets, change of control or otherwise" without prior written consent, "which may be withheld
in its sole discretion," and that any attempted assignment "is void." The library says clauses like
that are enforced as written, and "sole discretion" hands Hensley leverage to renegotiate
(`library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`). Buyer's Schedule 3.3 currently reads **"None."**
That is false on the face of your own data room, and we will not sign it.

The money: 0.38 × $4,600,000 = **$1,748,000** of revenue; on two independent valuation bases the
Hensley relationship is worth ≈ **$1,178,000** of the $3,100,000 price (both bases converge — math
in `apa_redline.md` §3.3). You told us the owner is a long-time personal friend, **has not been
told about the sale**, and "won't love a corporate buyer." So:

- **You call the owner first, person to person.** Our redline (§3.3(d)) blocks the buyer from
  contacting Hensley on its own before that happens. Do not let anyone from Lone Star call ahead
  of you.
- If Hensley refuses and the deal closes anyway without the MSA, expect the buyer to demand a
  **price reduction — our fallback range $[500,000]–$1,178,000** — or to walk, and either way your
  **earn-out goes to zero** on the math in item 3.
- We will also schedule Cascade (consent-free, notice-only — data room §1.2), the 22 residential
  contracts (data room §1.3), and the shop lease (§3.1; landlord consent "not unreasonably
  withheld") on Schedule 3.3. Small items, but they belong there.

## 3. The non-compete — the heaviest thing *you personally* are signing

§8.2 as drafted, verbatim: **"Seller and Ray Brightline shall not compete in the custom cabinetry
business within 500 miles of Austin for 7 years."**

You said: "I'll sign whatever non-compete, I'm retiring." Retirement is your plan; the signature
is still yours, and the library says 7 years / 500 miles for a local custom-cabinet shop is
**likely excessive in both dimensions**, with 3–5 years within the trade area typical
(`library/tx_noncompete_sale_of_business.md`). Our counter: **5 years** (fallback 3), scoped to
Travis County, contiguous counties, and counties where Brightline actually worked in the last 24
months; it should bar **owning or operating** a competing shop, not hiring you as an employee; and
it needs a **consulting carve-out** in case "retiring" turns into consulting. The library also
warns that an over-broad covenant invites IRS scrutiny of any consideration allocated to it — and
the file contains **no allocation schedule at all** (Q6), so we cannot even say what that covenant
is paying you.

And the earn-out you may be counting on is mostly an illusion: §2.4 pays 40% of EBITDA **above
$700,000 for the 12 months following Closing** (not calendar 2026), max $400,000. The maximum
requires $700,000 + $400,000 ÷ 0.40 = **$1,700,000** of EBITDA — 1,700,000 ÷ 740,000 = **2.30×**
your adjusted 2025 figure. Flat at $740,000 the payout is 0.40 × ($740,000 − $700,000) =
**$16,000**; on the unadjusted books ($518,000) it is **$0** — and §2.4 lets the **buyer** compute
EBITDA "in accordance with Buyer's accounting policies." Realistic value of the earn-out:
**$0–$16,000**, and if Hensley is lost there is no path to the floor: even keeping every add-back,
$740,000 − $281,200 (Hensley's margin-consistent EBITDA share) = $458,800, below $700,000. The
redline rewrites §2.4; that rewrite matters more than the headline percentage.

---

## So — can we just sign it?

**Not as drafted.** Signing today's draft means: (1) you *represent* your installers are properly
classified when your own data room reads the other way; (2) you agree that breach of that rep is
capped at the **full $3,100,000**, not the $310,000 escrow; (3) you agree the buyer's **knowledge
of the problem protects you zero** (§7.4(c)); and (4) that claim can arrive after the escrow is
gone. That is how a roughly $150,000–$240,000 known issue becomes a $2,790,000-beyond-escrow
problem. Separately, the Hensley consent has **never been sought** and it is the critical path of
the deal; the spray-booth permit (data room §4.1) is non-transferable and takes 30–60 days.

**Signing in two weeks is realistic** if the §3.3 / §4.12 / §7.4 fixes in our redline are agreed
now, with you opening the Hensley conversation immediately. **Closing** in two weeks is not
realistic — consents and the permit gate that, and the timetable should be built around them
(Outside Date in the redline). Nothing in the redline is a deal-breaker for the buyer; every ask
is the library's own prescription for exactly these problems.

— deal counsel

All legal points above cite only the seven memos in `library/INDEX.md`; anything not in that
library is labelled **[unverified — not in library]**. Facts are from the data room extract, the
buyer's draft, and your own emails/answers. No fact was invented to fill a gap — the remaining
gaps are Q1, Q3–Q10 in `QUESTIONS.md`.

the library lists but doesn't quantify (SUTA, §3509 gross-up, penalties) gives ≈ **$236,400**.

confirm (Q10). Your confirmed 45–50 busy-season hours fit the pay data: $68,000 average annual
pay ÷ $37.50/hr midpoint = 1,813 hrs/yr = 33–50 hrs/wk over a 40–50-week year — busy-season-heavy,

in its sole discretion," and that any attempted assignment "is void." The library says clauses like
that are enforced as written, and "sole discretion" hands Hensley leverage to renegotiate

redline rewrites §2.4; that rewrite matters more than the headline percentage.

classified when your own data room reads the other way; (2) you agree that breach of that rep is

the deal; the spray-booth permit (data room §4.1) is non-transferable and takes 30–60 days.

**Signing in two weeks is realistic** if the §3.3 / §4.12 / §7.4 fixes in our redline are agreed

gaps are Q1, Q3–Q10 in `QUESTIONS.md`.

# Reply to buyer's counsel (J. Whitaker, Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC)

Re: Brightline Cabinetry LLC — asset sale; buyer draft APA as received; your follow-up message
asserting §7.4(c) "is market" and §4.12 "a plain-vanilla compliance rep."
Prepared for seller. Answers to your cover-email questions (Schedule 3.3; WARN), our position on
§7.4(c), and responses to your follow-up.

All legal support below is drawn from the reference library in this file (`library/INDEX.md`);
points we could not verify there are marked **[unverified]**. Facts are from the data room as
indexed and from the buyer draft itself. We have assumed a **Purchase Price of $3,100,000**,
derived from your own §9.3 ("$310,000 (10%)") because no price appears in the materials circulated
— please confirm (it moves every dollar figure below).

---

## 1. Schedule 3.3 — it cannot be "None"

You wrote that you left Schedule 3.3 blank because "we understand there are no consent issues."
The data room does not support that. Schedule 3.3 must be completed before signature, with:

**Item 1 — Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement §18 (data room §1.1). Consent required; we treat
it as a closing item, not an efforts-only line.**

- Hensley is the largest customer at **38% of revenue** (`0.38 × $4,600,000 = $1,748,000`), term
  2024–2028.
- §18 bars assignment "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise"
  without prior written consent, "which may be withheld in its sole discretion," and makes any
  purported assignment **"void."**
- The library: such a clause "is enforced according to its terms; an asset sale transferring the
  contract without consent is a breach and the transfer is void where the clause so provides," and
  a "sole discretion" consent "gives the counterparty leverage to renegotiate price"
  (`library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`: *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458
  (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §317, §322).
- Our redline therefore: (a) Schedule 3.3 lists Hensley; (b) Hensley's written consent (or an
  agreed carve-out with a conforming price adjustment) is a **condition to both parties' obligation
  to close**; (c) consent outreach is **seller-led** — the seller has the relationship and manages
  the approach, and our §3.3(d) draft bars unilateral buyer contact with Hensley before the seller
  has made the introduction; (d) an Outside Date governs the consent window. We ask Buyer to
  confirm in writing that it will take the MSA **on its existing commercial terms through 2028** —
  that confirmation is what makes the consent obtainable.
- Status: outreach has begun in the manner described; we will keep you informed at each milestone.
  Nothing about the relationship makes consent impossible; it makes sequencing matter.

**Item 2 — Cascade Builders framework agreement (data room §1.2; 11% of revenue ≈ $506,000).**
Assignment "permitted to a successor to substantially all assets upon notice." List it on
Schedule 3.3 with the notice as a pre-closing deliverable. This one is easy; we list it so nobody
pretends it doesn't exist.

**Item 3 — the 22 residential contracts (data room §1.3), "silent on assignment."** The library:
absent anti-assignment language, assignment of rights is generally permitted; obligations require
consent only if performance is personal (`anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`). Please produce
**Schedule 3.1(c)** — the Assigned Contracts schedule is referenced in §3.1 but was never
circulated. We will flag any contract whose performance names Brightline personnel.

**Item 4 — shop lease, 7700 Burleson Rd (data room §3.1; lease §22).** Landlord consent required
for assignment, "not unreasonably withheld." Schedule it; we will obtain it.

A draft that assigns "all assets … including the Assigned Contracts" (§3.1) while Schedule 3.3
says "None" gives Buyer a ready-made indemnity claim on day one and gives your client a closing
it cannot deliver. That helps no one.

## 2. WARN — confirmed, no notice required

Per the library (`library/warn_act.md`: 29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1); 20 C.F.R. §639.3): WARN applies to
employers of **100 or more employees** and to closures/mass layoffs of **50+ employees at a single
site**. Brightline has **14 W-2 employees** (data room §2.1: 7 shop, 4 installers, 3 office). Even
counting the nine 1099 installers as employees — we take no position on classification for this
answer — the total is **23**, far below both thresholds. **No WARN notice is required**, and the
library confirms **Texas has no mini-WARN statute**. Buyer's post-closing hiring decisions are
Buyer's own WARN question going forward; as to this transaction, you are under threshold.

## 3. §7.4(c) and the classification package — our answer to "it's market"

You wrote: *"7.4(c) is market, every deal has it. And 4.12 is a plain-vanilla compliance rep — if
Ray's contractors are fine, what's the concern?"* Three responses:

**(a) We do not dispute the label; we dispute the combination.** Our redline **keeps §7.4(c)**. The
problem is that §7.4(c) sits between a **clean §4.12 rep** and the **§7.4(b) carve-out** that caps
§4.12 at the full Purchase Price. The library states the consequence precisely: "Sellers who
disclose a known issue (e.g., contractor classification) in diligence and then give a clean
representation subject to a pro-sandbagging clause **have effectively agreed to indemnify for the
disclosed issue**. The seller's protection is either (i) an anti-sandbagging clause, (ii) a
disclosure schedule exception to the representation, or (iii) a special indemnity with a negotiated
cap — **not a clean rep**" (`library/sandbagging.md`). We are offering exactly (ii) and (iii). If
7.4(c) is "market," then so is the library's market summary on caps: ~10% for general reps, and a
specific operational rep like worker classification carved out to a full-price cap is
**"off-market and should be resisted or replaced with a sized special indemnity"**
(`library/baskets_caps.md`). Your draft pairs an "every deal" clause with a clause the library
calls off-market. Pick one.

**(b) §4.12 is not untrue because we say so; it is untrue on Buyer's own data room.** The concern
is not hypothetical. Data room §2.2 — compiled by your deal team's diligence list — describes nine
installers "working exclusively for Brightline, using Brightline trucks and tools, scheduled daily
by the shop foreman, paid hourly ($34–41/hr), for an average of 3.4 years," with "no written
contractor agreements." The library's classification memo says individuals who work "exclusively
for one business, on its schedule, with its tools and vehicles, paid hourly, for years" are
employees under the common-law control test **regardless of the label**, and flags successor
exposure and IRC §3509 consequences (`library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md`: Rev. Rul. 87-41;
Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1; IRC §3509; Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134). A "plain-vanilla"
rep cannot be squared with a data room that reads like the library's fact pattern; asking the
seller to rep it clean while carving it to full price and keeping pro-sandbagging converts a
known, disclosable issue into an uncapped bet against the seller.

**(c) The numbers, so the ask is calibrated.** Our scenario table (`apa_redline.md` §4.12):
employer FICA 7.65% × $612,000/yr = $46,818/yr, × 3 years = $140,454; FUTA 9 × $7,000 × 0.6% =
$1,134; FLSA overtime premium on 5–10 OT hrs/wk × $34–41/hr × 0.5 over 12/20/26 busy-season weeks
= $3,060–$15,990. Three-year totals: **$144,648–$157,578**; with a 50% allowance for the items the
library cites but does not quantify (SUTA, §3509 gross-up, penalties, interest) ≈ **$236,400**.
(Rates and the 3-year window are flagged assumptions — the library cites IRC §3509 and the TWC
provisions but not the rates or the limitations period **[unverified]**.) Against that, §7.4(b)
sets the cap at $3,100,000 — **$2,790,000 beyond the escrow**, roughly **13×–21×** the realistic
exposure (3,100,000 ÷ 236,367 ≈ 13.1; ÷ 144,648 ≈ 21.4). And §7.4(d) keeps the rep alive to the
limitations period + 60 days while the escrow releases at 18 months (§9.3).

**Our position, concretely:**
1. Preferred: **Schedule 4.12 exception** disclosing the data room §2.2 facts; §4.12 then subject
   to the general $310,000 Cap; §7.4(c) stays as you drafted it.
2. Fallback: §4.12 stays clean, but (i) a **new §7.5 special indemnity for classification/tax
   exposure capped at $[250,000], escrow-only**, survival tied to escrow release; (ii) §4.12 back
   inside the general Cap for everything else; (iii) if Buyer keeps pro-sandbagging, the special
   indemnity is the *only* route for classification Losses.
3. Either way, "Fundamental Representations" must be **defined** — §7.4(b) caps them at the
   Purchase Price but the circulated sections never define the term; an undefined exception to the
   Cap is worse than a defined one.

## 4. Timing — sign in two weeks is achievable; plan the closing around consents

We can sign in two weeks if the §3.3 / §4.12 / §7.4 package above is agreed in this round.
Closing is a different date: Hensley's consent (or the agreed carve-out) gates it, and the City of
Austin **spray-booth permit is non-transferable, reapplication 30–60 days** (data room §4.1) — so
the timetable needs an Outside Date and, if you want to close before the permit issues, an interim
operations protocol. None of our asks is a delay tactic; the redline keeps your structure and
prices the known risks instead of pretending they are zero.

## 5. Items we need from Buyer

1. The full APA: definition of **"Purchase Price"** (does it include the earn-out? the §8.2
   covenant consideration?) and of **"Fundamental Representations"** (undefined in what we
   received).
2. **Schedule 3.1(c)** (Assigned Contracts) and the **allocation schedule**, if any exists.
3. Written confirmation of Buyer's intent to take the Hensley MSA on existing terms through 2028.
4. Your underwriting's number for the classification exposure, so the special-indemnity size can
   be set against a real figure instead of dueling scenarios.

— seller's counsel
